**Note on the source:** I couldn't load the Metaculus page (question 45330), so I can't tell you what it currently says. Everything below comes from news and polling sources.

## Status quo
- The current government is a National–ACT–NZ First coalition led by PM Christopher Luxon. The election is scheduled for 7 November 2026. That's three weeks from today (18 Oct).
- Seats at the 2023 election: National 48 (38.06%), Labour 34 (26.91%), Greens 15, ACT 11, NZ First 8, Te Pāti Māori 6. A majority needs 61 of 120 seats.
- Luxon was weakened earlier this year: on 12 Aug 2026 he survived a second party leadership vote.

## Recent polls (newest first)
- **1News–Verian, 8–12 Oct (released 13 Oct):** Hipkins and Luxon are tied at 20% as preferred PM. Party support held largely steady, and Opportunity remains kingmaker: neither bloc can govern without it. The headline says Opportunity is on track for 10 MPs. Luxon has ruled out working with Opportunity before and did so again that day.
- **Taxpayers' Union–Curia, 1–5 Oct:** National 28.5%, Labour 28.2% (up 2.3), Greens 13.3%, NZ First 12% (up 3.6). Curia also does internal polling for National. RNZ's headline said the poll showed the coalition extending its lead.
- **1News–Verian, 1–5 Oct:** National 29, Labour 28, Greens 16, NZ First 10, ACT 9, Opportunity 7. The right bloc would have 58 seats, with Opportunity holding the balance of power on eight seats.
- **RNZ–Reid Research, 24 Sep–1 Oct:** Labour 30.8, National 25.9, Greens 14.8, NZ First 10.6, ACT 9, Opportunity 5.5. This was the left bloc's first lead over the right in any poll since June.
- **Earlier:** Roy Morgan (31 Aug–27 Sep) had National 31 and Labour 23.5. Freshwater (4–11 Sep) had Labour 28 and National 27. Anacta (4–10 Sep) had Labour 31 and National 30.

## What this means for the outcome
- The race is effectively tied, and the result likely turns on Opportunity (leader Qiulae Wong), which is polling around 5–7%. Two things follow:
  - **If Opportunity holds the balance of power:** Luxon has ruled it out, which points toward Labour–Green–Opportunity (Labour-led).
  - **Opportunity's 5% threshold:** If it falls below 5%, its seats disappear and the right bloc (National–ACT–NZ First) is favoured. A National-led government is also possible if the right wins an outright majority.
- An "Other"-led government is very unlikely. No party besides Labour or National has ever led an MMP government.
- No prediction-market prices were found in this search.

## Timing and the "None before January" risk
- Official results, including special votes, usually come out about 2–3 weeks after election day, so around late November.
- In 2023, a 14 Oct election produced a government sworn in on 27 Nov, about 6 weeks later. In 2017 it took about 5 weeks. In 1996 talks took about 8 weeks.
- From 7 Nov, a similar 6–8 week gap runs to late December or early January. That makes "None before January" a real tail risk if talks are three-way and drawn out, especially with Luxon refusing to deal with Opportunity.

## Scheduled events
- More weekly polls (1News–Verian, Curia, Reid, Roy Morgan) and further leaders' debates before 7 Nov.
- Election day on 7 Nov, official results in late November, then coalition talks.

## Current lean
On current information, the outcome is a toss-up. Recent polls slightly favour a Labour-led government if Opportunity clears 5%, and a National-led one if it falls short.

criterios:
This question will resolve according to the New Zealand government following the 2026 parliamentary elections based on the following criteria:

* **Labour-led**, if the government formed is led by the Labour Party irrespective of which other parties are in coalition.
* **National-led**, if the government formed is led by the National Party, irrespective of which other parties are in coalition.
* **Other**, if the government formed is led by a party other than the Labour or National Party.

If no government is formed before January 2027, this question will resolve as **None before January**.

The New Zealand Government will be the primary source for resolution, such as the seating plan for the 55th Parliament.

razonamientos:
(a) **Time left until the outcome is known:**
The general election is scheduled for 7 November 2026 (~20 days away). Official vote counts (including special votes) conclude in late November. Government formation typically concludes between late November and mid-to-late December, or January 2027 if protracted (approximately 5 to 11 weeks from today).

(b) **Status quo outcome:**
A National-led government (currently the governing coalition comprising National, ACT, and New Zealand First under Prime Minister Christopher Luxon).

(c) **Base rates or historical frequencies:**
Under MMP in New Zealand (since 1996, 10 general elections):
- Every single government formed has been led by either National (1996, 1999–partially transitional, 2008, 2011, 2014, 2023: 5 of 10) or Labour (1999, 2002, 2005, 2017, 2020: 5 of 10). "Other"-led governments have a base rate of 0%.
- Duration of negotiations: The time between election day and swearing-in has ranged from roughly 33 days (2017) to 44 days (2023) and 65 days (1996). With an election date of 7 November, 54 days remain before 1 January 2027. Negotiations exceeding ~7.5 weeks across the Christmas/New Year holiday period represent a ~10–20% historical risk when talks are multi-party and contested.

(d) **Unexpected outcome scenario:**
The Opportunity Party (TOP) clears the 5% threshold and holds the balance of power, while Christopher Luxon refuses to negotiate with them and Labour's concessions to the Greens and TOP prove unpalatable to moderate caucus members. Negotiations drag past Christmas into the New Year without an agreement, resulting in no government being sworn in before January 2027, or leading to an unprecedented arrangement such as a short-term minority government led by a cross-bench figure or an unresolved caretaker period extending into January.

***

(a) **Time left:** The election is on 7 Nov 2026, about 3 weeks away. Official results with special votes should come around late November. Coalition talks would then likely end in December, so the answer should be known within roughly 6–10 weeks. That means by early January at the latest.

(b) **Status quo:** The current government is National-led (National–ACT–NZ First). Polls show a near tie. Opportunity is the kingmaker, and National has ruled it out. If polls stay where they are and Opportunity clears 5%, the arithmetic points to a Labour–Green–(Te Pāti Māori)–Opportunity arrangement. If Opportunity misses 5%, the right bloc is favoured.

(c) **Base rates:**
- Every New Zealand government under MMP has been led by Labour or National, so "Other" is very rare.
- Small parties like TOP (now Opportunity) have historically underperformed their polling: 2.4% in 2017, 1.5% in 2020 and 2.2% in 2023. Polls of 5.5–7% now carry real downside risk.
- Government formation has taken about 4–8 weeks after election day. From 7 Nov, that runs to mid/late December, with some spill-over risk into January.
- Incumbent-led blocs in tight New Zealand races have split roughly evenly.

(d) **Unexpected scenarios:**
- Opportunity wins about 6% and refuses to formally back either side, while Te Pāti Māori is internally unstable. Three- or four-way talks then drag past Christmas and nobody is sworn in before January.
- Alternatively, National reverses its ruling-out of Opportunity after the election, or replaces Luxon and deals with Opportunity to stay in power.

**Weighing it:**
- I put Opportunity's chance of clearing the threshold at about 60–65%.
- Even above 5%, a Labour-led government is not certain, because Labour also likely needs Te Pāti Māori.
- Below 5%, the right bloc is fairly likely, though not certain.
- Overall it is near a toss-up, with a slight lean to the incumbent bloc given small-party underperformance.

**Time to resolution:** The election is 20 days away, on 7 November 2026. The outcome should become clear during coalition negotiations, potentially in December; the “None before January” option remains possible until 1 January 2027.

**Status quo:** If the current governing arrangement survived the election and negotiations, the result would be **National-led**.

**Base rates:** Labour and National have each led five of the ten governments formed after MMP elections since 1996. Incumbents have remained in government after six of those elections. All ten governments formed before the following January, though past elections do not eliminate the risk of unusually prolonged talks this time.

**Unexpected-outcome scenario:** Opportunity wins pivotal seats, but neither major party can reach an agreement with it. Negotiations extend into January—or National reverses its refusal to work with Opportunity and remains in power.

The polls describe a close race. I give Labour a modest edge because Opportunity appears capable of clearing the 5% threshold and National has ruled out governing with it. National’s incumbency and the possibility that Opportunity falls short keep National-led government a substantial prospect.
